steps.prompt: Is $221$ prime? How far do you have to check before you can be sure?

cards.title: Building blocks
cards.body: A prime has exactly two divisors, $1$ and itself: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots$ ($1$ is not prime, and $2$ is the only even prime). Every whole number above $1$ splits into primes in exactly one way, like $360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$. Build the factor tree by pulling out small primes first.

cards.title: Worked example: a factor tree
cards.problem: Write $360$ as a product of primes.

steps.text: Halve while you can: $360 \to 180 \to 90 \to 45$. That is three $2$s.

try.prompt: How many times can you halve $360$ and still get a whole number?

cards.title: Testing for a prime
cards.body: If $n$ is not prime, it has a prime factor no bigger than $\sqrt{n}$. So to test $n$, try only the primes up to $\sqrt{n}$. For $221$, $\sqrt{221} < 15$, so try $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13$.

steps.text: $14^2 = 196$ and $15^2 = 225$, so we only need primes up to $14$: the largest is $13$.

try.prompt: What is the largest prime you need to try?

steps.text: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11$ fail, but $221 = 13 \times 17$. So $221$ is not prime.

cards.title: The common trap: 1, 2 and hidden factors
cards.body: $1$ is not prime. $2$ is prime, and it is the only even one, so if two primes add to an odd number, one of them is $2$. Numbers like $91 = 7 \times 13$ and $143 = 11 \times 13$ look prime but aren't: check every prime up to the square root.

prompts: Which numbers look prime but aren't? Name one and its factors.
